description:
This Orb-weaver’s web is adhered to the vertical surface of a giant boulder- Madison Boulder, second largest glacial erratic in the United States, in Madison, New Hampshire.

I wasn’t careful photographing this spider, and the photo came out blurry. I assumed it was Araneus diadematus (Cross Spider), which are relatively common in my area, so I didn't think I needed a great shot of this one. But looking closely at the photos at home and comparing them to others online, I realized I may have Araneus nordmanni, which for me would be a lifer. Now I am kicking myself for not taking better pictures. I don’t usually like to post photos of inferior quality to iNat, as it makes identifying difficult, but as this is potentially a lifer, I’m throwing it out there for any arachnophiles to back up my ID.

description:
I was out spider hunting one night in a forested area, not finding much until I happened upon a bright yellow, sizable orb-weaver. I did not recognize the species and I got excited at the thought of photographing a lifer. I was careful as usual, but I must have jostled a branch or a line of silk in the web because I startled the spider who immediately retreated to it’s hide in a curled up leaf at the top of the web. I was very frustrated at having missed my photo opportunity. I knew it was unlikely she would be coming out again any time soon. I continued spider hunting in the area, but close enough so that I could make my way back to the small tree the web was built on to see if she had re-appeared. Returning to look two times, she did not appear, and I finally had to leave.

After that, it haunted me. I wondered if I could return and find a nondescript tree in a pitch-black forest at night. A little more than two weeks later, I was in the area again and decided to give it a shot.

I retraced my path as well as I could. I had a hope of success because although there wasn’t a trail, the terrain I traveled the last time was distinctive, and there were features like ridges and small valleys, and various objects like old appliances that provided landmarks of a sort. About three-quarters of the way in I started to lose landmarks and thought I might not be able to find the tree I was looking for, but a short distance further and there it was! And the spider was there, in the center of her web.

Finding it was just the first hurdle. Last time I had startled the spider into hiding. This time I moved as slowly and carefully as I could so as not to jostle anything. Having come all this way, I was very nervous about scaring her away again, but I got enough shots that when I inevitably startled it and it crawled up into its hide, I was okay with it. But then I got lucky again. A fly flew into the web, triggering the spider to return to the web to dispatch and wrap its prey. It gave me an opportunity for more photos. I was even able to take some video of it.

So it was a complete success and a heck of a lot of fun. A little bit of an adventure that contributes to why I enjoy the hobby of photographing spiders.

At home, I identified it as a Marbled Orb-weaver which I had never seen or photographed before. If my identification is correct, it is a lifer! Icing on the cake of a very good day.

A few notes on the photos. Picture 7 is looking up inside the curled leaf the spider used as a retreat. You can just see a blurry yellow dot inside the leaf.

Pictures 8 and 9 show the curled leaf at the top of the photo, and some of the tangle web below it, adjacent to the orb-web. This tangle web in association with the orb-web made me initially think the spider might be a Labyrinth Spider in the genus Metepeira, but colors, markings, behavior, and location are better matched by Araneus marmoreus. It may be that the tangle web to the side of the orb is just used to curl the leaf which the spider used as a hide.

She set up basecamp on the window of an Airbnb door Burien, WA. 

This appears to be a cross orbweaver (Araneus diadematus), one of about 180 species in North America. 

Cross orbweavers are also referred to as crowned orbweavers and diadem spiders: dorsal markings glimmer like jewels in the night with a camera flash. There is a cross-like pattern toward the top of the dorsum. 

Orb weavers are the most common type of spider with over 3,000 species worldwide. Orb weavers are known for spinning webs with concentric circles and radial lines of silk, including a dragline to escape danger.
